full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondent herein, as writ petitioner filed the Writ Petition No.1108 of 2006 challenging the Assessment of Customs and duties vide Nathi No.5-Cus-12(198)Group-4 /Gari/2004 dated 27-10-2004 of the car in question on the basis of fixed price instead of value of the car as was fixed in the import invoice value and bill of entry stating that Mr Phutachart Chaiwatana, the then Deputy Trade Commissioner of France Embassy in Bangladesh as diplomatic privileged person import a Marcedes Benz car bearing chassis No. WDB-12024-2A553980 engine No.103 Model 12604, Horse Power-3000 CC Mgf year 1990, price USA $ 4,275 through bill of entry No.C-42303 dated 28-11-2001 invoice No. 371 dated 13-9-2001, B/L No.JEA-CGP-1000058 dated 20-10-2001 without any tax and on payment of assessment fee of Taka 410 vide assessment notice bearing file No.1632/ AP/SEC-8 (B)01-02 dated 29-11-2001 of Chittagong Customs House and registered the said vehicle in Bangladesh bearing registration No.Da-51-102. Mr Phutachart Chaiwatana after competition of his assignment in Bangladesh while was intending to leave Bangladesh, he sought permission for selling out the aforesaid Mercedes Benz car to Mr Yahya AZ Khondoker, the writ petitioner from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Government of Bangladesh. Upon the prayer of Mr Phu tachart Chaiwatana, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh, accorded permission of sale of the Mercades Banz in question to the writ petition vide letter bearing memo No.(Ms-1)-3/51-03 dated 10-6-2004 and thereafter said Mr Phutachat Chaiwatana handed over all the necessary documents to the writ petitioner. 

 3. Being emboldened by the letter dated 10-6-2004 of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh, the writ petitioner on 12-6-2004 submitted all the original document of the said Merecdes Benz Car to the office of the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Dhaka and prayed for assessing Customs and duties leviable under the Customs Act. On receiving the application from the writ petitioner, the Commissioner of Customs, Dhaka vide its letter bearing Nathi No.5-Cus-12(198) Group-4/4675 dated 17-6-2004 sought to know the genuineness of the imported value to the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong who vide its letter bearing Nati No. 1632/AP/Section-8(B)/2001/8484- Cus, dated 30-6-2004 opined that at that time, they were assessing the customs duty of car of 2004 like the car in question at Euro 42,500. After receiving all the necessary documents of the said car, (Commissioner of Customs vide Nathi No.5-CUS-12(198) group-4/Gari/2004/ 6247 dated 10-8-2004 also sought the opinion of the National Board of Revenue for assessing the Customs duties and on receiving the letter dated 10-8-2004 of the Commissioner of Customs, the National Board of Revenue vide Nathi No.5(3) Bibhid/Shulko Jatri-o-Kut Naitik subidha/2002/600 dated 20-9-2004 directed the Commissioner of Customs to assess the customs duties of the said car as per law prevailing in the land especially mentioning the date of importation of the said car in Bangladesh i.e. 28-11-2001. 

 4. Inspite of receiving said letter dated 20-9-2004 of the National Board of revenue with the direction to assess the customs duties as per law of the land, the customs authority without assessing the customs duties as per law i.e. standing order bearing No.100 of 2000 of the National Board of the Revenue which clearly enjoins to assess the customs and duties of any imported car on the basis of import invoice value and bill of entry of the said car but the custom authority with malafide intention to harass the writ petitioner most illegally and unwarrantedly assessed the customs duties at Taka 41,42,502 fixing the price of the said car at USA $ 73,155.61 vide title No. 5, Cus/12 (198) Group-4/Gri/04 dated 27-10-2004 of Customs house, Dhaka dated 27-10-2004 which is equivalent to the price of Brand New car, though the said car is an used car of 14 years and thereafter, forwarded a letter to that effect dated 27-10-2004 to the writ petitioner which is without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect. 

 10. Mr Humayun Kabir, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the assessment has been made as per provisions of the Valuation Rules, 2000 and since invoice value always may not bear the actual transaction value for various reasons, the Customs Authority should not be compelled to accept the invoice value for assessment purpose for the sake of Government Revenue. As in the present case, at the time of 1st importation of the Mercedes Benz Car no duty and taxes was paid by the importer as per Exemption Certificate No. France 82/2001, the High Court Division without considering these things made the Rule absolute. He further submits that, the High Court Division wrongly decided that, the valuation of the Car in question has been made in 2004 at Euro 42,500 which was valued by the same customs authority in 2001 at US $ 4,275 overlooking the facts that, in 2001, the Car was released without any duty/tax and just on receipt of assessment fee of Taka 410 by assessment notice dated 29-11-2001 and thus, committed error of law in declaring the assessment dated 27-10-2004 as illegal. He lastly submits that the High Court Division in declaring the assessment dated 27-10-2004 as was passed without lawful authority created hurdle in receiving the revenue of the Government, but, the High Court Division committed serious illegality in making the Rule absolute with some directions and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

 11. Per contra, Mr TM Shakil Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submits that, the standard order No.100 dated 25-7-2000 issued by the National Board of Revenue and relevant law and submitted that assessment on the basis of the aforesaid opinions, which referred to a brand new Car of similar model and made of 2004 was erroneous and arbitrary. He further submits that, the writ respondent No.2, the Commissioner of Customs fell in serious error in ignoring the assessed value of the Car on the bill of entry dated 28-11-2001 in assessing the customs duty and/or tax etc and such assessment was, therefore, unauthorized and illegal. Hence, the High Court Division rightly passed the impugned judgment and order and, therefore, he prays for dismissal of the instant appeal. 

 "The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the assessment has been made as per the provisions of the valuation Rules, 2000 and since invoice value always may not bear the actual transaction value for various reasons the Customs Authority should not be compelled to accept the invoice value for assessment purpose for the sake of Government Revenue. As in the present case, at the time of 1st importation of the Mercedes Benz car no duty and taxes was paid by the importer as per Exemption Certificate No. France 82/2001 the High Court Division did not consider these things and made the Rule absolute which is liable to be set-aside. 

 He lastly submits that the High Court Division in declaring the assessment without lawful authority dated 27-10-2004 as was passed created hurdle in receiving the revenue of the Government." 

 14. The pivotal point raised by the appellants and to be decided herein is that whether the importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value applicable on the date of production of bill of entry. 

 15. In the case of Mustafa Kamal and others vs The Commissioner of Customs and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 1 this Division observed that: "Section 30 then provides that both the value and the rate of duty applicable to any imported goods shall be those on the date on which bill of entry is presented under section 79 of the Customs Act." 

 "It is now a settled principle of law that whatever may be the position on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit but the importer is saddled with the liability to the taxes and duty prevalent on the date of filing of the bill of entry. In the case of Mustafa Kamal vs Commissioner of Customs and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 1 it has been held— 

 The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of bill of entry. 

 In the instant case, the tariff value was prevalent on the date of filing of the bill of entry and, as such, liable to pay duty, etc. on the basis of tariff value. This view is supported by a decision of this Court in the case of Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 wherein it has been held— 

 As the present case is under section 25(7) of the Customs Act we are of the view that customs duty is payable by the importer respondent on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice or tariff value in force at the time of opening of Letter of Credit. So, the decision in 50 DLR (AD) 40 appears to us to be not correctly decided due to the failure of the then Attorney-General to point Out the distinction between 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 on the one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other." 

 17. In the present case Bill of entry was presented on 28-11-2001 and the car was manufactured in the year of 1990. As such, appraisal of the customs And duties of the car under consideration produced in the year of 1990 fixing its price at US $ 73,155 as a spanking new Car of 2004 is anything but legal and with lawful authority. Such whimsical conduct cannot be sustained before law. 

 18. We too find merit in the submission as to that the Customs Authority has assessed the Customs Duties of the Car in contravention of the condition of the standing order No.100 of 2000 of the National Board of Revenue. 

 19. Regarding the very last submission as to that the High Court Division in declaring the assessment without lawful authority dated 27-10-2004 as was passed, created hurdle in receiving the revenue of the Government, it is true that a revenue generating issue of the state is the matter of higher State interest cannot be defeated for the sake of procedural glitches. Albeit, this must be borne in everyone's mind and work too that Government in its generic sense is not a merely business or commercial entity in the realm of crony capitalism. It is a super-institution which initiates the laws and policies for the whole country and such laws are to be obeyed by everybody including Government itself. In this connection Government are not entitled any upper hand over everyone else. It too obliged to conform to the rule of law. It as well emerged as a general position that when customs duty is imposed for any intention, the authority to do so is the Parliament as Article 83 of our Constitution speaks that "No tax shall be levied or collected except by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament". As such, for the sake of generating revenue, Government is not exempted from following strict rules of laws. Governments too have to earn revenue within the legal scheme established by the State coupled with its citizen's rights and interest. Procedural fairness too should be observed on the very face of it instead of whim. Consequently, we find no merit in this submission.
